subject: physics
title: Momentum (HT only)
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Momentum (HT only) — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.5.7.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Momentum (HT only), specification section 4.5.7.
final_note: You worked through Momentum (HT only) — 18 specification statements.

concepts.def: A property of a moving object, defined by the specification as an equation: momentum is mass multiplied by velocity. Because velocity appears in the definition, an object has momentum only while it is moving, however large its mass is.
The word equation that defines momentum. It is one of the equations students must recall, so it has to be learned rather than looked up, and both quantities must be in SI units before it is used.
The symbol form of the definition: p stands for momentum, m for mass and v for velocity. Writing the symbols out before substituting keeps momentum separate from F = m × a, which shares the symbol m.
The unit of momentum. It is a compound unit built from the units of the two quantities being multiplied: kilograms for mass and metres per second for velocity, so kg × m/s = kg m/s.
In p = m v the mass, m, must be in kilograms. A mass quoted in grams or tonnes has to be converted first: divide grams by 1000, multiply tonnes by 1000.
In p = m v the velocity, v, must be in metres per second. A speed quoted in km/h is converted by dividing by 3.6. Velocity also has a direction, so momentum has a direction too.

A system in which no mass enters or leaves and no external resultant force acts. Conservation of momentum is stated by the specification for a closed system, and it is that condition which makes the total momentum before and after an event equal.

The name given to the statement that, in a closed system, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after the event. It applies to the total for the whole system, not to each object separately.

Anything that changes how the objects in a system are moving: a collision, objects sticking together, or an explosion pushing objects apart. Momentum is used as a model to describe and explain what happens in such an event.

An event in which objects initially at rest push each other apart. The total momentum before is zero, so the total momentum after must also be zero: the two objects move in opposite directions with momenta of equal size.
Newton's second law: the resultant force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration. It is one of the two equations the specification combines to obtain the momentum form of the law.
The acceleration equation: acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken. Substituting it into F = m × a is what produces the momentum form of the second law.
The quantity m ∆ v, the mass multiplied by the change in velocity. Because momentum is m v, multiplying the same mass by the change in velocity gives the change in momentum, in kg m/s.
The equation formed by combining F = m × a with a = (v - u)/(t). The force equals the change in momentum divided by the time over which that change happens.

How quickly momentum changes, that is the change in momentum divided by the time taken. The specification states that force equals the rate of change of momentum, so the same change spread over a longer time means a smaller force.

When a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move, the object's momentum changes. The force changes the velocity, and since momentum is mass × velocity with the mass fixed, the momentum must change with it.

Air bags, seat belts, gymnasium crash mats, cycle helmets and cushioned playground surfaces. Each one increases the time taken for the change in momentum to happen, which reduces the rate of change of momentum and so reduces the force.

mcqs.q: The specification defines momentum by an equation. Which word equation is that definition?
options: momentum = mass × acceleration
momentum = weight × velocity
momentum = mass × velocity
momentum = force × velocity
mcqs.explain: This is the defining word equation given in 4.5.7.1, and it is one of the equations students are required to recall.

mcqs.q: Which symbol equation for momentum does the specification give?
options: p = m × a
p = ½ m v²
p = m v²
p = m v
mcqs.explain: The symbol form printed in 4.5.7.1: p for momentum, m for mass, v for velocity.

mcqs.q: Which unit does the specification give for momentum, p?
options: kilograms metre per second, kg m/s
kilogram per metre second, kg/m s
newtons per second squared, N/s²
newton metres per second, N m/s
mcqs.explain: The unit printed in 4.5.7.1, and the one built by multiplying kg by m/s.

mcqs.q: A ball has a mass of 400 g and travels at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?
options: 2 kg m/s
80 kg m/s
0.4 kg m/s
2000 kg m/s

mcqs.q: A lorry's speed is given as 54 km/h. What must be done before this value is used in p = m v?
options: It must be converted to metres per second, by dividing by 3.6, because v in p = m v is in m/s
It can be put straight into p = m v as 54, because km/h is already a unit of speed
It can be substituted just as it is, provided the mass of the lorry is given in kilograms
It must be multiplied by 3.6, the number that converts between the two units of speed
mcqs.explain: The specification gives velocity, v, in metres per second, so a speed in km/h has to be converted first.

mcqs.q: A skateboarder of mass 60 kg moves at 4 m/s. What is the skateboarder's momentum?
options: 15 kg m/s
0.067 kg m/s
240 kg m/s

mcqs.q: A 40 000 kg lorry moves at 3 m/s. A 1200 kg car moves at 30 m/s. Which statement is correct?
options: The car has the greater momentum, because it is the faster moving of the two vehicles
They have equal momentum, since the lorry's extra mass is cancelled by the car's extra speed
The lorry has the greater momentum: 120 000 kg m/s against only 36 000 kg m/s for the car
The lorry has the greater momentum, because momentum simply depends on a vehicle's mass
mcqs.explain: 40 000 × 3 = 120 000 kg m/s and 1200 × 30 = 36 000 kg m/s, so the lorry's momentum is larger.

mcqs.q: A trolley of mass 5 kg has a momentum of 12 kg m/s. What is its velocity?
options: 60 m/s
mcqs.explain: Rearranging p = m v gives v = p / m = 12 / 5 = 2.4 m/s.

mcqs.q: Why is the unit of momentum kilograms metre per second?
options: Because it is the unit of force multiplied by the unit of the time for which that force acts
Because momentum is mass × acceleration, so the unit is kg multiplied by m/s² instead
Because momentum is a compound quantity, so its unit is always a compound unit too
Because momentum is mass × velocity, so the unit must be kg multiplied by m/s, or kg m/s
mcqs.explain: The unit of any quantity comes from the equation defining it: kg × m/s = kg m/s.

mcqs.q: The specification states conservation of momentum for a closed system. What is a closed system?
options: One in which the objects are all sealed inside a container, so that nothing can escape from it
One in which no mass enters or leaves and no resultant force acts on it from outside the system
One in which nothing is moving, so that the total momentum of the system stays equal to zero
One in which the objects touch each other, so that momentum can be passed from one to another
mcqs.explain: This is the condition under which the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it.

mcqs.q: In a closed system the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. What is this called?
options: Newton's third law of motion
Conservation of net force
Conservation of momentum
Conservation of energy
mcqs.explain: This is the name the specification gives to the statement in 4.5.7.2.

mcqs.q: Two skaters stand at rest on ice and push each other apart. Which statement about their momentum is correct?
options: They have equal and opposite momenta, so the total is still zero, as it was before the push
Both of the skaters are now moving, so the system has gained momentum from the push they gave
Each skater simply keeps the momentum it began with, which was zero for both
Their momenta add together, giving twice the momentum that one skater has on its own
mcqs.explain: The total momentum before the push is zero, and in a closed system the total after must also be zero.

mcqs.q: A moving trolley collides with a stationary trolley and slows down, while the second trolley moves off. Which description is correct?
options: Some momentum was destroyed in the collision, which is why the first trolley slowed down
Each trolley keeps the momentum it began with, since momentum is a conserved quantity
The momentum lost by the first trolley equals the momentum gained by the second, so the total is unchanged
The second trolley gains momentum but the first loses more, so the total falls in the collision
mcqs.explain: In a closed system the total momentum before the event equals the total momentum after it.

mcqs.q: (physics only) A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg trolley. They stick together. What is their velocity after the collision?
options: 4 m/s
12 kg m/s
mcqs.explain: Momentum before = 3 × 4 = 12 kg m/s. Afterwards the moving mass is 5 kg, so v = 12 / 5 = 2.4 m/s.

mcqs.q: (physics only) A 0.5 kg ball moving at 8 m/s hits a stationary 1.5 kg ball. The first ball stops. What is the velocity of the second ball?
options: 8 m/s
12 m/s
4 kg m/s
mcqs.explain: Momentum before = 0.5 × 8 = 4 kg m/s. All of it passes to the 1.5 kg ball, so v = 4 / 1.5 = 2.7 m/s.

mcqs.q: (physics only) A 50 kg skater at rest pushes a 15 kg sledge away at 4 m/s. What is the skater's velocity after the push?
options: 4 m/s backwards
1.2 m/s backwards
13.3 m/s backwards
60 kg m/s backwards
mcqs.explain: The total momentum stays zero, so 50 × v = 15 × 4 = 60, giving v = 1.2 m/s in the opposite direction.

mcqs.q: (physics only) A resultant force acts on an object that is free to move. What does the specification say happens?
options: The object's momentum is transferred into the force, which is why the object slows down again
The mass of the object changes, since momentum is mass × velocity and the momentum changes
The object's velocity changes but its momentum does not, because its mass is unchanged
A change in momentum occurs, because the force changes the object's velocity in that time
mcqs.explain: 4.5.7.3 states that when a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move, a change in momentum occurs.

mcqs.q: (physics only) Which two equations does the specification combine to give F = (m ∆v)/(∆t)?
options: F = m × a and a = (v - u)/(t)
p = m a and a = (v - u)/(t)
F = m × a and a = ∆v × ∆t
F = m × a and E = ½ m v²
mcqs.explain: These are the two equations named in 4.5.7.3; substituting the second into the first gives the momentum form.

mcqs.q: (physics only) Which statement describes the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) correctly?
options: The force equals the change in momentum, m ∆ v, multiplied by the time over which it changes
The force equals the change in momentum, m ∆ v, divided by the time taken for that change
The force equals the time taken divided by the change in momentum that occurs during it
The force is simply the change in momentum, m ∆ v, whatever the time it takes
mcqs.explain: m ∆ v is the change in momentum, so the equation says force equals the rate of change of momentum.

mcqs.q: (physics only) In the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), what does the quantity m ∆ v represent?
options: The force acting on the object, because force equals the change in momentum
The change in momentum, that is the mass multiplied by the change in velocity
The total momentum the object had before the force began to act on it, in kg m/s
The change in the force acting, which is the mass multiplied by the change in acceleration
mcqs.explain: The specification states directly that m ∆ v = change in momentum.

mcqs.q: (physics only) The specification says force equals the rate of change of momentum. What does 'rate of' add?
options: Nothing of substance; the force is simply equal to the change in momentum that takes place
That the momentum is multiplied by the time for which the resultant force acts on the object
That the change in momentum is divided by the time taken for that change to happen
That the momentum changes at a steady rate whenever any resultant force acts on an object
mcqs.explain: 'Rate of' means per second, which is why ∆t appears on the bottom of F = (m ∆v)/(∆t).

mcqs.q: (physics only) Why does an air bag reduce the force on a passenger during a crash?
options: It reduces the passenger's change in momentum, so there is less momentum to be got rid of
It absorbs most of the force of the crash, so that only a little of it reaches the passenger
It brings the passenger to rest more quickly, before they can strike anything solid nearby
It increases the time taken for the change in momentum, lowering the rate of change
mcqs.explain: The same change in momentum spread over a longer time gives a smaller force, from F = (m ∆v)/(∆t).

mcqs.q: (physics only) A gymnast lands on a crash mat rather than on the bare floor. Why is the force on the gymnast smaller?
options: The mat soaks up much of the force of the landing, so that only a small share of it reaches the gymnast
The mat reduces the gymnast's momentum before the landing, so there is less momentum to be removed
The mat lowers the gymnast's mass on impact, so the change in momentum m ∆ v is made smaller
The mat squashes, so the momentum falls to zero over a longer time, making F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) less
mcqs.explain: The change in momentum is the same either way; the mat increases ∆t, which reduces the force.

mcqs.q: (physics only) A 70 kg passenger moving at 12 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s without an air bag, and in 0.6 s with one. What are the two forces?
options: 84 N and 504 N
8400 N and 504 N
840 N and 840 N
